newsitem.title: MONGOLIA: Mongolian opposition stronger in local poll win.
newsitem.headline: Mongolian opposition stronger in local poll win.

text.p: Mongolia's opposition former communists urged the newly elected democratic government to boost cooperation after claiming victory in local polls, four months after a crushing defeat in general elections.

Preliminary, unofficial results showed the formerly communist Mongolian People's Revolutionary Party (MPRP) with 55 percent of the vote in Sunday's local elections. The ruling Democratic Union Coalition took the remaining 45 percent.
Official results of the polls to elect 7,535 representatives to councils, or Hurals, at the provincial and district levels, would be announced on Thursday, the Election Committee said.

"These latest elections showed that the MPRP is one of the strongest parties in the country and can't be ignored," party general secretay Enkhbayar said in an interview. "Therefore, the government should cooperate and work with us."
The ex-communists said they expected to control the People's Hurals, or provincial councils, in at least 15 of the 21 provinces as well as Ulan Bator municipality.
In elections last June for the Great Hural, or parliament, the MPRP suffered a crushing defeat, winning just 25 seats in the 76-seat parliament, compared with their previous 70.
The Democratic Union Coalition swept to victory with 50 seats, ending 75 years of rule by the communists and their heirs in this former satellite of the Soviet Union.
The MPRP had controlled the regional and local councils until Sunday's elections. In the last vote for such bodies in 1992, the democrats won just four percent of the vote.
Despite its loss of influence in the local councils, the MPRP said it viewed the results of Sunday's election as "positive" following its defeat in June.
"It's a very strong opposition", Ganbold, general-secretary of the Democratic Union Coalition, said in an interview.
He said the pace of the democrats' reforms was not at risk, with most power centralised in the hands of the government.
On cooperation with the opposition, Ganbold said: "This is not a new question. We already work with them in the framework of a multi-party system and in the parliament."
One main result of the local elections was a more balanced political scenario, said one Western diplomat.
Enkhbayar said the MPRP would pose not threaten government reforms intended to lead Mongolia from a Soviet-style economy to a free market.
"People in Mongolia understand that democracy and market economy are the only way to develop the country and keep its independence," he said.
The Democratic Union Coalition stands for faster reforms and in its June election campaign had sharply criticised the slow pace of reforms implemented by the MPRP govermnent.
Turnout in Sunday's elections was 64.2 percent, compared with 92.15 percent in the June polls.
Many voters who did not cast their ballots were people who had voted for the democrats in June but were dissatisfied with their performance in power, another diplomat said.
